source: Lowe, Baker, Fillmore (1997) A Frame-Semantic Approach to Semantic Annotation
finding: States the core theory: word meanings are understood against conceptual structures (frames) that act like stereotyped scenarios. A frame has frame elements (roles).
numbers: Example: Commercial transaction frame with BUYER, SELLER, PAYMENT, GOODS; words buy, sell, pay, charge, customer, clerk each evoke it.
quote: word meanings are best understood in reference to the conceptual structures which support and motivate them
limits: Descriptive paper, no test of psychological reality. Authors say they make no cognitive claim about frames and use the term formally.
agent_relevance: S1/S2: restate a task as a frame by listing its roles (who, what, to whom, with what). Any role the text leaves blank is a gap to ask about or flag.

source: Lowe, Baker, Fillmore (1997) A Frame-Semantic Approach to Semantic Annotation
finding: Frames encode schematised real-world knowledge, not only linguistic knowledge. Frames form hierarchies and subframes inherit elements from parents.
numbers: Example: RealEstateTransaction inherits CommercialTransaction with links BORROWER=BUYER, LOAN=PAYMENT; adds LENDER. Buying a candy bar vs buying a house with a mortgage evoke different subframes and attach 'with' phrases differently.
limits: Hand-built examples. The authors do not know in advance how much world knowledge must be put in frames.
agent_relevance: Frame choice changes how ambiguous phrases attach. The agent should pick the most specific frame it can justify, then inherit roles from the parent frame.

source: Fillmore (1976, 1977) Frame semantics and the nature of language; Scenes-and-frames semantics
finding: Early papers separate scene (a cognitive or experiential entity) from frame (a linguistic one). Later work drops 'scene' and calls a frame a cognitive structuring device indexed by words (as reported by Petruck, via search snippets).
numbers: Scenes-and-frames semantics: Zampolli (ed.) Linguistic Structures Processing, pp. 55-81, 1977.
limits: Not opened; secondary description only. Attribution of the commercial-event example to 1977 vs 1982 differs across secondary sources.
agent_relevance: Keep the experience of a situation (scene) separate from the linguistic frame. A task text is one frame view of a scene and may hide roles.

source: Fillmore (1982) Frame semantics (Linguistics in the Morning Calm, Seoul: Hanshin, pp. 111-137)
finding: The canonical statement of frame semantics. Meaning of a word is not defined by truth conditions alone but by the background frame a speaker needs to understand it.
numbers: Citation facts only: 1982, pp. 111-137.
limits: Not opened (paywalled / not retrieved). Content cited second-hand through Baker et al. and Lowe et al.
agent_relevance: Cite as origin of the frame idea in S1; do not rely on its claims beyond what opened sources repeat.

source: Fillmore (1985) Frames and the semantics of understanding, Quaderni di Semantica 6:222-254
finding: Contrasts understanding semantics (U-semantics, based on frames) with truth-conditional semantics (T-semantics) (per Petruck, via search snippets).
numbers: Quaderni di Semantica vol 6, pp. 222-254.
limits: Not opened. Only secondary descriptions seen.
agent_relevance: Supports the schema choice that understanding a task means filling a frame, not just checking truth of a statement.

source: Baker, Fillmore, Lowe (1998) The Berkeley FrameNet Project
finding: Describes the start of FrameNet: frame elements (FEs) are local to a frame, unlike global theta-roles. Frames get frame-description tools, annotated corpus sentences and a lexical database. Valence is recorded as Frame Element Groups (FEGs).
numbers: At project year 2: about 10,000 sentences annotated for just under 200 lemmas, about 20,000 FE tokens, about a dozen frames specified. Plan: 5,000 lexical units, about 250,000 sentences, over 500,000 FE tokens.
quote: frame elements, are local to particular conceptual structures
limits: Planning numbers, not final. Later releases are far larger (see Chundru et al.: FN 1.7 over 1,200 frames, 13,000 lexical units).
agent_relevance: Role names tied to the frame (DRIVER, VEHICLE) give a richer slot list than generic Agent/Patient. Schema S1 slots should be task-specific.

source: Baker, Fillmore, Lowe (1998) The Berkeley FrameNet Project
finding: Worked example of frame specialisation: TRANSPORTATION has MOVER, MEANS, PATH. DRIVING adds DRIVER and VEHICLE and may add CARGO or RIDER. RIDING_1 makes RIDER the main mover.
numbers: Not numeric. Different subframes allow different syntactic realisations (DRIVER or VEHICLE can be subject; PATH and VEHICLE can be objects).
limits: Author-built analysis.
agent_relevance: Subframe choice decides which role is the controller. Agent should state that before planning.

source: Gildea & Jurafsky (2002) Automatic Labeling of Semantic Roles. Computational Linguistics 28(3)
finding: First statistical system to label frame elements in FrameNet sentences. A probabilistic classifier on features (phrase type, grammatical function, parse path, head word, voice, position).
numbers: Data: 67 frames, 12 domains, 1,462 predicates (927 verbs, 339 nouns, 175 adjectives), 49,013 sentences, 99,232 frame elements. Role labeling of given constituents: 82% accuracy (abstract), 80.4% (final, frame-specific roles) vs 40.9% baseline P(r|t). Identify and label FEs: 65% precision, 61% recall; whole sentence all-correct 38%.
limits: Early FrameNet data, gold frames and targets. 13% of FEs have no matching parse constituent, which caps results.
agent_relevance: Parsing a text into a frame is learnable, but errors at boundary finding dominate. Check role spans, not just role types.

source: Gildea & Jurafsky (2002) Automatic Labeling of Semantic Roles
finding: Frame-specific roles and 18 collapsed thematic roles perform about the same, so the classifier is robust to role-set granularity. Lexical statistics matter most, and clustering or WordNet fixes sparse head-word data.
numbers: Abstract thematic roles 82.1% vs frame roles 80.4%. Lexical head-word P(r|h,pt,t) 87.0% accuracy but only 41.6% coverage. Clustering of NPs 83.4% to 85.0%; WordNet NPs 84.3%; overall 80.4% to 81.2%. Adding 156,590 self-labelled sentences: coverage 41.6% to 54.7%.
limits: Roles from a small corpus; sparse data was the main problem.
agent_relevance: Coarse roles may be enough for the agent. Fine frame-specific roles help mostly when there is data about them.

source: Gildea & Jurafsky (2002) Automatic Labeling of Semantic Roles
finding: Frame-element groups carry strong priors, and joint prediction of all roles of a sentence beats labelling each role alone. Example: blame in Judgment frame.
numbers: Distribution for blame: {Evaluee, Judge, Reason} 0.549; {Evaluee, Reason} 0.167; {Evaluee, Judge} 0.160; {Evaluee} 0.097.
limits: Single-verb example. Priors are corpus-specific.
agent_relevance: Optional roles are often left out in real text. An empty role is common and not an error on its own, so the agent should ask only if the role matters to the answer.

source: Das, Chen, Martins, Schneider, Smith (2014) Frame-Semantic Parsing. Computational Linguistics 40(1)
finding: SEMAFOR: two-stage model. Stage 1 frame identification with latent variable and semi-supervised lexicon expansion. Stage 2 argument identification with exact dual decomposition enforcing frame constraints (no overlapping roles, excludes and requires relations).
numbers: SemEval 2007, frame ID with gold targets: exact 60.21 F1, partial 74.21. Full parse with automatic targets about 4.4 F1 above Johansson&Nugues 2007 baseline. FrameNet 1.5, gold targets: 82.97 exact, 90.51 partial. Gold frames argument F1 79.08 naive vs 79.88 beam 10,000; full model 68.45.
limits: Supervised, feature-based; SemEval is a small noisy set.
agent_relevance: Role constraints (excludes, requires) are cheap code checks. Our S1 frame check can be rule-based in the program, not the model.

source: Das et al. (2014) Frame-Semantic Parsing
finding: Error is mostly in frame identification and unseen words. Wrong frame costs a lot downstream; unseen targets are hard.
numbers: FN 1.5: 50.1% of test targets ambiguous; exact accuracy on them 73.10%, partial 85.77%. 144 of 4,458 targets unseen: 23.1% exact, 46.6% partial. Latent-variable ablation: model without it drops significantly (exact 80.30 vs 75.54 rows in Table 5 compare supported-feature variants). Perfect vs predicted frames: about 22 F1 drop (18 with partial credit). Most-frequent-frame baseline 74.0 to 88.1%.
limits: Most-frequent-frame baseline is strong, so gains are modest on frequent words. Table 5 row labels were garbled in extraction.
agent_relevance: Picking the frame is the high-risk step. Agent should list at least two candidate frames for ambiguous trigger words and check one against context.

source: Das et al. (2014) Frame-Semantic Parsing
finding: Local argument prediction yields structurally bad outputs; global decoding fixes this. The constraint 'at most one overt argument per role' holds for 96.5% of role instances.
numbers: SemEval 2007 training data 96.5% and FN 1.5 full text 96.4% of role instances have at most one overt argument. LP relaxation tight 99.8% of the time on test. Naive 68.09 F1 vs beam 68.46 on the full-parse setting reported in text.
limits: Constraint statistic is for English SemEval and FN 1.5 text.
agent_relevance: A uniqueness check (one filler per role) is a valid cheap G2/G3-style code check on slot filling.

source: Swayamdipta, Thomson, Dyer, Smith (2017) Frame-Semantic Parsing with Softmax-Margin Segmental RNNs and a Syntactic Scaffold
finding: Open-SESAME: first syntax-free neural frame-semantic argument identifier (segmental RNN, recall-oriented softmax-margin). A syntactic scaffold (Penn Treebank multitask at train time only) gives state-of-the-art without a parser at test time.
numbers: FN 1.5 test, argument ID with gold frames: SEMAFOR 59.1 F1; FitzGerald 2015 63.1; Open-SESAME about 62.9 (single) and 64.6 (ensemble); ensemble with dependency features 65.3. Earlier heuristics based on predicted dependencies bounded recall below 72.6%.
limits: Gold targets and frames; FN 1.5. Column alignment in the extracted table is approximate.
agent_relevance: Explicit syntax is not needed to fill frames. Suggests the LLM may fill roles without a separate parse step.

source: Kabbach (2017/2019) Debugging Frame Semantic Role Labeling (replication on FrameNet 1.7)
finding: Replication of argument-identification results. The reported baselines replicate, but preprocessing (POS tagger, dependency parser) changes F1 by about as much as recent model gains. Gains from extra training data and hierarchy features replicate smaller on FN 1.7.
numbers: Replication on FN 1.5: 75.6 F1 (SEM) vs Roth&Lapata 75.7; ACL script 60.1 vs 59.1 for Kshirsagar 2015. NLP4J tagger: +0.3 (test) to +0.7 (dev) F1. Dependency parser change: +1.3 to +2.6 F1. Exemplar sentences added: +1.2 F1 vs +2.8 originally. Hierarchy feature: +0.5 to +0.7 vs +1.3 originally; another feature +2.4 vs +4.
limits: Master-level memoir, not peer reviewed. Only argument identification studied.
agent_relevance: Small F1 gains in the literature are near noise from pipeline choices. Our G7 rule (pay for itself at equal tokens) applies to frame steps too.

source: Kabbach (2019) Debugging Frame Semantic Role Labeling
finding: Reviews domain shift: argument identification drops about 20 F1 out of domain (Johansson & Nugues 2007). Das et al. argued exemplar sentences could not train parsers on SemEval data; later work found a few F1 points gain.
numbers: Exemplar sentences are more than 3 times the size of full-text data, yet gains stay limited. Historical record: 76.6 F1 argument ID with predicted frames (Yang & Mitchell 2017), 68.9 with gold frames (Swayamdipta 2017).
limits: Different splits and scoring scripts make numbers hard to compare (the author's own point).
agent_relevance: Beware numbers from different scorers. Domain shift hurts frame filling, so check roles again when the task type changes.

source: Garat, Moncecchi, Wonsever (2025) Exploring In-Context Learning for Frame-Semantic Parsing
finding: Prompts built only from FrameNet definitions and examples let LLMs do frame identification (FI) and role labeling (FSRL) with no fine-tuning. Six LLMs: Claude Haiku 3.5, Claude Sonnet 3.5, GPT-4o, GPT-4o mini, DeepSeek Chat, DeepSeek Reasoner.
numbers: Best FI F1 94.3% (frame 95.3%, target 94.3%, DeepSeek Chat, 100 shots). Best FSRL with gold frame-target 77.4% (DeepSeek Reasoner, 150 shots); previous supervised FN 1.7 range 75.56-77.06%. Chained FI+FSRL: large models 78.0-82.5%, small 66.8-78.5%.
limits: Limited frame subset because of prompt length; not directly comparable with full-benchmark supervised systems; annotation inconsistencies in the gold data.
agent_relevance: With frame definitions in the prompt, an LLM fills frames about as well as trained parsers on a few frames. Supports S1 writing the task as a frame, if the frame inventory is small.

source: Garat et al. (2025) Exploring In-Context Learning for Frame-Semantic Parsing
finding: Experiment 1 on the single Killing frame: zero-shot is weak, examples help a lot. Knowledge in pretraining plus frame definitions alone is not enough.
numbers: Claude Sonnet 3.5 best 82.9% F1 at 250 shots; GPT-4o 80.2% at 400; Claude Haiku 71.1% at 275; GPT-4o mini 68.7% at 375. Zero-shot to best: +30 to +41 F1. Arguments: Target 97.0, Victim 83.3, Killer 71.4, Cause 68.1, rest at most 50.0 (large) and below 22.2 (small). 100 evaluated examples.
limits: One frame and 100 test examples; wide uncertainty. Location argument never occurs in the test set.
agent_relevance: Core roles (Victim, Killer) are filled well; peripheral roles (Means, Instrument, Place) are filled badly. Agent should treat peripheral slots as low-reliability.

source: Garat et al. (2025) Exploring In-Context Learning for Frame-Semantic Parsing
finding: Ablation: giving the frame definition improves results, especially for the full parsing task; benefit depends on model and task complexity. DeepSeek Reasoner with only task text and frame definition beat its own zero-shot baseline on the end-to-end task.
numbers: Prompt variants: (a) no FrameNet info, (b) frame definitions only, (c) frame plus argument definitions, (d) best shots. Experiment 3a F1 by model at best shots ranges 67.1-77.4.
limits: Exact ablation table cells not individually extracted here. Small frame set.
agent_relevance: Roles listed with definitions in the prompt matter. Provide the slot list, not just the frame name.

source: Devasier, Mediratta, Li (2025) Can LLMs Extract Frame-Semantic Arguments? (EMNLP 2025)
finding: Zero-shot and few-shot LLMs do poorly on FrameNet argument extraction, but fine-tuned open LLMs beat earlier supervised systems. Output format matters: JSON listing only existing frame elements was best.
numbers: FN 1.7 split: train 3,353 sentences / 19,391 frames / 34,219 FEs; test 1,247 sentences / 6,714 frames / 11,302 FEs. Few-shot F1: GPT-4o-mini 0.471; DeepSeek V3 0.548; GPT-4o 0.592; prior SOTA 0.771 (Ai&Tu); KAF-SPA 0.813 listed in table; fine-tuned Qwen 2.5 72B +3.9 F1 over prior SOTA; JSON-Existing +3.4 F1 and +4% precision vs other formats.
limits: Strict exact-match metric; closed LLMs prompted, open ones fine-tuned with LoRA, so training data differs.
agent_relevance: Un-tuned LLMs are far below tuned systems at exact role extraction (0.47-0.59 vs 0.77). Do not trust a raw LLM frame fill; use code checks (G2).

source: Devasier, Mediratta, Li (2025) Can LLMs Extract Frame-Semantic Arguments?
finding: Generalisation: unseen frames hurt modestly, unseen frame elements hurt a lot, and out-of-domain text is worse than the old SEMAFOR.
numbers: Unseen frame: -7.7 F1 vs overall. Unseen FEs: -27.0 F1. YAGS out-of-domain: GPT-4o F1 0.387, Phi-4 (fine-tuned) 0.533, SEMAFOR 0.570. Fine-tune data scaling: 1% 0.508, 5% 0.619, 10% 0.688, 25% 0.746, 100% 0.785. Instruction-tuned Qwen 7B 0.703 vs base 0.768. GPT-4o-made instructions 0.225 vs manual 0.471.
limits: Several settings tested one model at a time (sequential tuning). Automated-instruction result may be specific to GPT-4o prompts.
agent_relevance: New role names are the failure point, so for a new task type the agent should define roles by their meaning. A model writing its own frame instructions did worse than a hand-written one.

source: Devasier et al. (2025) Can LLMs Extract Frame-Semantic Arguments?
finding: Benchmark correlation: models good at multi-step reasoning (MuSR) do better at argument identification; instruction-following (IFEval) correlates negatively.
numbers: Benchmarks used: IFEval, BBH, GPQA, MuSR, MMLU. Exact correlation values not recorded here.
limits: Few models in the correlation sample; correlation is not cause.
agent_relevance: Role filling may use reasoning ability more than prompt-following. Fits a program-led frame check rather than a prompt rule.

source: Chundru, Poddar, Cao, Jiang (2025) Do LLMs Encode Frame Semantics? Evidence from Frame Identification
finding: Prompted LLMs identify the frame of a target word well without training. Fine-tuned Llama-3.1-8B (QA format) matches the state of the art in-domain.
numbers: FN 1.7 accuracy: zero/few-shot prompts about 80.0-83.5%; fine-tuned 91.9%; earlier supervised SOTA about 92.5-92.6 (COFFTEA 92.5, KGFI 92.1). FN 1.5: prompts 82.4-83.3%; fine-tuned 91.7%. Averages over 3 runs.
limits: Candidate frames are given (lexicon-filtered), so this is choosing among options, not open frame discovery.
agent_relevance: Choosing among listed candidate frames is reliable; open frame invention is harder. S1 should offer candidate frames.

source: Chundru et al. (2025) Do LLMs Encode Frame Semantics?
finding: Out-of-domain and object-to-function frames: tuned model generalises on YAGS but only reaches half on Artifacts. LLM-generated frame definitions work almost as well as gold definitions.
numbers: YAGS: 80.7% (fine-tuned). Artifacts (938 objects, prototypical function): 25.6% zero-shot to 49.6% after fine-tuning. Generated definitions: Llama-3.1-8B 75.0 zero-shot, DeepSeek-V3.1 79.3, GPT-4o 80.0, FN 1.7 gold-definition run 78.4-79.3. Frame names sometimes beat full definitions; best few-shot 83.5% with frame names and LU definitions. Error overlap with FIDO: 538 vs 519 errors, 320 shared, 296 same wrong frame.
limits: Generated-definition table layout is ambiguous in the extracted text; read the numbers as approximate. Shared errors suggest label-set subtleties, not only knowledge gaps.
agent_relevance: A model can write the frame definition itself and use it. But errors are correlated with other systems, matching G4 (agreement is not proof).

source: Belcavello et al. (2025) Evaluating the Impact of LLM-Assisted Annotation in a Perspectivized Setting: FrameNet Annotation
finding: Human-only vs LLM-parser-only (LOME) vs human correcting LOME for FrameNet-style annotation. The hybrid raised frame diversity and kept coverage; the machine-only setting was much worse except for speed.
numbers: 12 documents, 311 sentences. Average time per sentence: human 14.96 min vs hybrid 12.97 min (1.99 min saved, small). Annotators discarded 19.68% of machine annotation sets and fully accepted 6.61%; 17.5% of hybrid sets were created from scratch. Core FEs annotated fell to 90.65% in hybrid.
limits: Small sample, 12 documents; Brazilian Portuguese FrameNet (1,429 frames, 13,071 FEs); LOME is not a current frontier LLM. Under peer review when posted.
agent_relevance: Machine frame suggestions widen what a human notices but do not make work much faster. Use model frame-fills as prompts for review, not as final.

source: Rehbein et al. (2009), as reported in Belcavello et al. (2025)
finding: Earlier study of pre-annotation for frames and roles: annotators were faster with pre-annotation but not significantly so. Belcavello et al. say their time result replicates this.
numbers: No numbers recorded here; only the 'not statistically significant' summary seen second-hand.
limits: Not opened; reported through Belcavello et al.
agent_relevance: Pre-filled slots do not clearly save effort; they can anchor the reviewer. Mind anchoring in S1.

source: Su et al. (2024), as reported in Devasier et al. (2025); and a PropBank-SRL study (DMR 2024)
finding: A Llama 2 zero/few-shot argument-extraction test reached very poor performance (per Devasier). A separate PropBank study found GPT-4 got only 42.9% accuracy on role assignment across syntactic realisations, few-shot (search snippet).
numbers: PropBank, not FrameNet: 42.9% few-shot accuracy with GPT-4. Su 2024: no number seen.
limits: Neither paper opened; Su model identity (Llama 2) is inferred from a snippet. PropBank is a different role scheme.
agent_relevance: Prompted role assignment is brittle across surface forms; a check is needed (G2/G3).

source: Hartmann et al. (2017), reported in Chundru et al. (2025)
finding: Showed domain generalisation problems of frame-semantic parsers and released the YAGS out-of-domain benchmark. Supervised parsers on FrameNet text lose accuracy on YAGS.
numbers: No numbers extracted; YAGS used by Devasier (SEMAFOR F1 0.570) and Chundru (fine-tuned 80.7% frame ID).
limits: Not opened; only named in related work.
agent_relevance: The standard test for frame-based understanding of new domains. Use similar held-out domains for any frame step we add.
